    on foot   by train or optional   The cherry blossom marks Ueno Park, the anchor near the flat; when it is off the map a blossom chip at the edge points to it. The gold chrysanthemum marks the Imperial Palace. Stop positions come from OpenStreetMap; the line joins the stops, so follow the campus paths on the ground.

    Gothic brick, an Edo garden and an AI laboratory

    Two hours on foot, every stop seen from outside.

    A walk of about two hours through the University of Tokyo's Hongō campus, from Hongō-sanchōme to Yushima. You walk about 3.2 km and see fifteen stops, all from outside. The campus is the old upper residence of the Maeda lords of Kaga. Most of what stands is Uchida Yoshikazu's rebuilding after the 1923 earthquake.

    Any day of the trip. The grounds are open to walkers 07:00–18:00 every day, without a pass; tell the guard at the gate you are visiting. Faculty buildings, Yasuda Auditorium and the library are closed to visitors. On Saturday and Sunday the main gate's big doors are shut, but its small side door is open 07:00–24:30. The university asks that photos stay personal: not posted on social media or published. No exam days fall in December.

    The leaves that week. The ginkgo avenue is usually at its brightest from late November to early December. In the first week of December expect either a full yellow canopy or a carpet of fallen leaves; one windy night can strip the trees. Around Sanshirō Pond the maples turn later than the ginkgo, so they may be red that week. No source gives the 2026 dates; check a few days before.

    The stops

    1Hongō-sanchōme station

    What it holds
    A station on the Marunouchi and Ōedo lines, at the Hongō crossing. The campus begins about 400 metres north.
    Designed by
    —
    Built
    —
    What the designer meant
    —

    From where you stand. Come up to street level and walk north on Hongō-dōri. The long wall that soon appears on your right is the edge of the old Maeda estate, now the campus.

    Can you go in? The station, yes. You can also start at Yushima and walk the tour backwards.

    2Akamon, the red gate (赤門)

    What it holds
    A gate, not a building. It is a National Important Cultural Property.
    Designed by
    No designer is named; it was built by the Maeda house.
    Built
    1827, when the Maeda lord Nariyasu married Yasuhime, a daughter of the shogun Tokugawa Ienari. The university received it in 1877. Closed since 12 February 2021 for earthquake strengthening; the university plans to reopen it in 2027.
    What the designer meant
    No statement of intent survives. The design itself says it: a vermilion gate of the kind a lord's house built to receive a bride from the shogun's family.

    From where you stand. Stand on the far side of Hongō-dōri and take in the red lacquer, the tiled roof and the two small guard wings. Just to its left, inside the wall, you can see the long low line of Fukutake Hall.

    Can you go in? No. The gate is shut until 2027, so walk on north to the main gate.

    3The main gate and the ginkgo avenue (正門・銀杏並木)

    What it holds
    The main entrance to the campus. The avenue of ginkgo trees runs from it straight to Yasuda Auditorium.
    Designed by
    The gate and guard house are by Itō Chūta. Uchida set the straight line of the avenue in his post-earthquake plan.
    Built
    Gate 1912. Its original doors and lintel were replaced with aluminium copies in 1988.
    What the designer meant
    No statement of intent by Itō was found. The university calls the gate a blend of Japanese spirit and Western technique (和魂洋才), a wooden gate in a mixed style.

    From where you stand. Stand in the gateway and look straight up the avenue: the trees frame the clock tower of Yasuda Auditorium at the far end. This is the view the whole plan was built around.

    Can you go in? Yes, on weekdays 07:00–18:00. At weekends use the small side door.

    4The Reppinkan and Engineering Building 1 (列品館・工学部1号館)

    What it holds
    The Reppinkan now holds the Faculty of Engineering offices; it was planned as a museum of research specimens. Engineering 1 is a teaching building and hosts engineering ceremonies; its light court became an indoor hall in 1996.
    Designed by
    Uchida Yoshikazu (the Reppinkan with Kishida Hideto, by some accounts). The 1996 work on Engineering 1 is by Kōyama Hisao.
    Built
    Reppinkan 1925, the first building finished under the rebuilding plan. Engineering 1 1935, on the site of Tatsuno Kingo's 1888 engineering college, which the 1923 earthquake damaged. Both registered as cultural property in 1998.
    What the designer meant
    No words of Uchida's own were found. The university says he devised this style as the style of the rebuilding, and the Reppinkan was its first example. A 2021 study by Tsunematsu Yūsuke argues he chose Gothic so new buildings would agree with the older campus.

    From where you stand. At the Reppinkan porch, look at the row of pointed arches and the tall narrow windows: every later building repeats them. At Engineering 1, count the thin piers between the windows; each one marks a column of the frame inside.

    Can you go in? No. Both are seen from outside.

    5Law Building 3 (法学部3号館)

    What it holds
    Teaching rooms of the Faculty of Law.
    Designed by
    Uchida Yoshikazu. A rooftop storey was added in 1976; in 2012 a new tower was set into the central courtyard, keeping the low old front.
    Built
    1927; registered as cultural property in 1998.
    What the designer meant
    No statement of intent found. The registration text says the east front stresses vertical lines to answer the axis that joins the General Library and Engineering 1, so the building takes its cue from the plan around it.

    From where you stand. Look at the arched entrance, which copies the Reppinkan opposite. Then look above the old roofline for the 1976 storey and the 2012 tower behind.

    Can you go in? No.

    6Law and Letters Buildings 1 and 2: the arcades (法文1号館・2号館)

    What it holds
    Teaching buildings for Law and Letters, facing each other across the avenue. The ground floor of each is a covered arcade used as a public path.
    Designed by
    Uchida Yoshikazu. The rust-brown steel vaults on both roofs are by Kōyama Hisao.
    Built
    Building 1: west part 1929, whole building 1935. Building 2: 1938. Rooftop vaults 1976–81. Both registered in 1998.
    What the designer meant
    The university says the arcade of Building 1 is meant to recall the inside of a church with a nave and two aisles, and carries on the pointed arches of the campus's older buildings. Of the roof vaults it says they were an addition meant to keep the design of the whole campus unified (キャンパス全体のデザインの統一を意図した増築).

    From where you stand. Step into an arcade and look along the row of pointed arches; this is the space the university compares to a church aisle. Back on the avenue, look up at the quarter-circle steel vaults sitting on the 1930s brick.

    Can you go in? Yes, through the arcades only; the buildings themselves are closed.

    7Yasuda Auditorium (安田講堂)

    What it holds
    The university's great hall, used for ceremonies, and the offices of the central administration.
    Designed by
    Uchida Yoshikazu with Kishida Hideto. (The university's own guide names only Uchida.)
    Built
    1925, paid for by the banker Yasuda Zenjirō. Medical students occupied it in June 1968; students held it barricaded until riot police cleared it on 18–19 January 1969, and the 1969 entrance exam was cancelled. Earthquake strengthening and restoration June 2013 to December 2014. Registered cultural property No. 1 (1996).
    What the designer meant
    No statement by the architects was found. The university's guide says the design draws on a Cambridge college gate tower, and that for a university turning itself into a modern comprehensive university, "Yasuda Auditorium was to be its new icon" (安田講堂こそ大学の新しいイコンとなるべきものであった).

    From where you stand. From the foot of the avenue, take in the dark red-brown tile, the central clock tower and the deep arched entrance. Then walk round the side to see the curved hall behind the tower.

    Can you go in? No. Inside is open only on occasional sign-up tours; none were found for December.

    8Engineering Building 2: the AI laboratory (工学部2号館)

    What it holds
    Engineering departments, and the Matsuo–Iwasawa AI laboratory, whose own contact page gives this building as its address.
    Designed by
    Uchida Yoshikazu for the old wing. The designer of the towers was not found.
    Built
    Old wing 1924, Uchida's first building on the campus, designed before the earthquake. The north part was later demolished for a high tower, and a second tower was built over the kept south part; the year was not confirmed.
    What the designer meant
    No statement of intent found. What you see is a choice to keep the 1924 front facing Yasuda Auditorium and build the new work above and behind it.

    From where you stand. Stand on the Yasuda side and look at the low 1924 front, then raise your eyes to the tower rising over it. This is where the sixth stage of the six revolutions tour sits: the intelligence revolution, inside a 1924 shell.

    Can you go in? No. The laboratory is not open to visitors; it teaches the public through online courses.

    9Sanshirō Pond (三四郎池)

    What it holds
    A strolling garden round a pond of about 3,600 square metres, with 808 trees of 71 kinds. Its formal name is the Ikutokuen Shinji-ike (育徳園心字池), "the pond shaped like the character 心 (heart)".
    Designed by
    Laid out for the Maeda lords of Kaga; no designer is named.
    Built
    Early Edo period. The shogun Iemitsu and his father Hidetada visited in 1629, so the garden is older than that; one university page gives 1638. In Natsume Sōseki's novel Sanshirō the hero and heroine meet here, and the name stuck.
    What the designer meant
    No statement of intent survives. It is a daimyo garden: thick trees close it in so it seems deeper and wilder than it is (the water is under a metre deep).

    From where you stand. From the water's edge, look for the heart shape in the outline and the paths and small bridges. The ten-metre drop hides the brick campus, so for a few minutes you are in the Maeda garden, not a university.

    Can you go in? Yes; it is open ground. The path down from Yasuda Auditorium is steep.

    10Medicine Building 2 and the hospital edge (医学部2号館・東大病院)

    What it holds
    Medicine Building 2 is the old main building of the Faculty of Medicine and houses its office. East of it are the University Hospital's wards and research buildings.
    Designed by
    Uchida Yoshikazu, as were several hospital buildings of the 1920s and 1930s, some with Kishida Hideto.
    Built
    1936 by one source, 1938 by another. A library wing was added in 1961; earthquake strengthening 2008.
    What the designer meant
    No statement of intent found. The 2021 study by Tsunematsu says that from the late 1920s Uchida varied the style to suit each building's neighbours, and Kishida brought in plainer modern touches.

    From where you stand. Compare this front with the Law and Letters buildings: the brick and the vertical lines are the same, but the arches are fewer and the ornament thinner. Look east down the slope to the hospital towers.

    Can you go in? No. The hospital is a working hospital; do not wander in.

    11The General Library and the fountain plaza (総合図書館)

    What it holds
    About 1.2 million volumes in the old building, the Memorial Room and third-floor hall restored to their 1928 design, and the Asian Research Library (2020). Under the plaza is the Library Plaza annex, with automated stacks about 40 metres deep for some 3 million volumes.
    Designed by
    Uchida Yoshikazu; the university counts it among his best works. The recent renovation was designed by the university with Kōyama Hisao's office.
    Built
    The old library burned in the 1923 earthquake fire, with about 560,000 volumes. John D. Rockefeller Jr. gave 4 million yen in 1924, and the new building opened in December 1928. The underground annex opened in 2017; the renovation was finished in November 2020.
    What the designer meant
    No words of Uchida's own were found. The university describes the front as "a row of books facing the plaza", with a grand stair leading up to a space recalling a Roman basilica.

    From where you stand. Stand by the fountain and read the front as a shelf of books standing upright. Then remember that the fountain plaza is the roof of the new underground library.

    Can you go in? Normally no; it is for members. The visitor rules could not be read, so treat it as outside only.

    12Fukutake Hall (福武ホール)

    What it holds
    The Interfaculty Initiative in Information Studies: a 200-seat lecture theatre, workshop rooms, and the café UT Cafe BERTHOLLET Rouge.
    Designed by
    Tadao Ando, his first building at the university. Paid for by a gift from Fukutake Sōichirō.
    Built
    Opened March 2008, for the university's 130th anniversary.
    What the designer meant
    The hall's own page explains the design: the site is a strip 100 metres long and 15 metres wide along the campus edge, so the building stays low to spare the old camphor trees on the boundary. A 100-metre concrete "Thinking Wall" faces the campus, making a sheltered strip where students gather; more than half the building is underground.

    From where you stand. Walk along the campus side of the Thinking Wall and notice how little of the building rises above the camphor trees. From here you can also see the back of the Akamon.

    Can you go in? Open weekdays 08:00–20:00, weekends for events only. It is not stated whether visitors may walk in; the café is your best reason to try.

    13Daiwa Ubiquitous Computing Research Building (ダイワユビキタス学術研究館)

    What it holds
    Laboratories for ubiquitous computing and the internet of things. Sensors on the building measure wind, radiation, dust, temperature and humidity.
    Designed by
    Kengo Kuma, then a professor of engineering here. The earth wall on the garden side is by the plasterer Hasado Shūhei. Paid for by Daiwa House.
    Built
    Begun October 2012, finished April 2014, opened May 2014.
    What the designer meant
    Kuma's office wrote that it aimed to break the campus image of hard concrete, metal and stone and make "a soft building of wood and earth" (木と土でできたやわらかな建築). A soft opening through its middle joins the lane in front to the Japanese garden behind, making "an organic, soft flow of light and wind" (有機的でやわらかい、光と風の流れ).

    From where you stand. From the lane by the Kasuga gate, look up at the cedar boards hung like overlapping scales. Then look through the opening in the middle of the building to the old Kaitokukan garden behind.

    Can you go in? The ground-level opening and the small plaza, yes. Inside, no public hours were found.

    14Entrepreneur Plaza: the startup building (東京大学アントレプレナープラザ)

    What it holds
    Thirty offices and laboratories for young companies spun out of the university, on seven floors.
    Designed by
    Not named. It was paid for by Nemoto Nobuo, founder of the wig maker Aderans, on university land, and passes to the university after 30 years.
    Built
    Finished May 2007.
    What the designer meant
    No statement of intent found.

    From where you stand. Look at an ordinary seven-storey block and remember it holds about thirty companies. The second incubator, the Entrepreneur Lab (2018), and the university's venture fund UTEC are in the South Research Building, 250 metres north up the hospital lane.

    Can you go in? No; tenants only. In 2018 the business press called this cluster "Hongō Valley" (本郷バレー), after KERNEL HONGO, an AI incubator a few minutes from the Akamon whose address could not be found.

    15Yushima station

    What it holds
    Chiyoda line, near the flat.
    Designed by
    —
    Built
    —
    What the designer meant
    —

    From where you stand. Leave by the Tatsuoka gate, which is always open, and walk east down Kasuga-dōri. The road drops off the Hongō plateau towards Ueno.

    Can you go in? Yes. About 8 minutes from the gate.

    The two-hour plan

    Times are minutes from the start. For example, a 09:30 start ends about 11:30. On Saturday, before the conference, the campus opens at 07:00.

    0:00Hongō-sanchōme station. Walk north on Hongō-dōri (5 min).
    0:05Akamon from across the road (5 min). Walk on north to the main gate (5 min).
    0:15Main gate, the ginkgo avenue, the Reppinkan and Engineering 1 (15 min).
    0:30Law Building 3 and the Law and Letters arcades (10 min).
    0:40Yasuda Auditorium, then Engineering Building 2 behind it (15 min).
    0:55Down the steps to Sanshirō Pond (15 min).
    1:10Up to Medicine Building 2 and the hospital edge (5 min).
    1:15The General Library and fountain plaza (10 min).
    1:25Fukutake Hall and the Thinking Wall; coffee if the café lets you in (10 min).
    1:35Through the Kaitoku gate to the Kuma building and the Entrepreneur Plaza (15 min).
    1:50Out by the Tatsuoka gate to Yushima station (8 min). Home about 2:00.

    Food. The central cafeteria under Yasuda Auditorium (中央食堂) is open weekdays 11:00–21:00 and weekends 11:00–14:00. The co-op shop is open weekdays 10:00–18:00 and Saturday 11:00–16:00.

    What could not be confirmed

    • Whether the ginkgo will still be on the trees in the first week of December 2026.
    • Whether the Akamon's closure notice (dated November 2025) still holds; the reopening is given as 2027.
    • Uchida's own words on why he chose Gothic; his 1968 recorded interviews exist but were not read.
    • The date of Medicine Building 2 (1936 or 1938) and the year and architect of the Engineering 2 towers.
    • Whether visitors may walk into Fukutake Hall's café, and the library's visitor rules.
    • KERNEL HONGO's address and whether it still runs; the designers of the Entrepreneur Plaza and Lab.
    • Stop positions come from OpenStreetMap; the Law and Letters stop is placed between the two buildings.
